opus-5.5.text:
I think mathematics is special for a few reasons. The first is that it's a domain where you can actually verify things. When a model claims it has proven something, there's a ground truth. The proof is either correct or it isn't. That's very different from a lot of other domains where judging quality is subjective and messy. So math gives you a clean, objective signal of whether the model is really reasoning or just producing something that sounds plausible.

The second reason is that math is, in a sense, pure reasoning. You strip away world knowledge and trivia and are left with the core question: can you take a few axioms and definitions, chain logical steps together, sometimes over very long horizons, and arrive somewhere new? That's exactly the capability we care about for general intelligence. If a model can sustain a coherent argument over pages and pages, catch its own mistakes, backtrack, try a different approach, that's a really strong indication of genuine thinking.

And third, math has this beautiful gradient of difficulty. You can go from grade-school arithmetic, to competition problems, to graduate-level exercises, all the way to open research questions that the best humans in the world have been stuck on for decades. So it's a benchmark that doesn't saturate easily. Every time the models get better, there's a harder rung on the ladder waiting for them. Personally, what I find most exciting is that we're starting to reach that last rung, where models aren't just solving problems we already know the answers to, but actually contributing something new to mathematics. To me that's the moment where AI goes from a tool that retrieves knowledge to something that can create knowledge, and math is the place where we'll see that most clearly first.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think mathematics is really special for a few reasons. The first one is that it's maybe the purest form of reasoning that we have. When you solve a math problem, there's no ambiguity about whether you got it right. The proof is either correct or it isn't. So it's a domain where you can actually measure progress very cleanly, which is rare. Most of what we care about with these models, like writing, giving advice, coding in a messy real-world codebase, is hard to evaluate. Math is not like that.

The second reason is that math has this incredible depth. You can go from arithmetic that a kid does, all the way up to open research problems that the best mathematicians in the world have been stuck on for decades. And it's a continuum. So as the models get better, you don't run out of benchmark. You just move up the ladder. We went from grade-school word problems, to competition math, to the olympiad, and now we're starting to look at things that look like real research-level questions. That same ladder doesn't really exist in most fields.

And the third thing, which I think people underestimate, is that math is not about memorization. You can't solve a new olympiad problem by having seen the answer somewhere. You have to actually find the idea. So when a model does well on a genuinely novel problem, it's telling you something real about its ability to reason, to search through a space of ideas, to recognize when it's on the wrong track and back off. Those are exactly the capabilities we care about everywhere else.

So for me, math is kind of the canary. If the models are making progress on hard math, I'm fairly confident that progress will show up in science, in engineering, in all these other domains, maybe with a little delay. And conversely, if they were stuck on math, I'd be worried about everything else too.

astra-6.text:
I think mathematics is a very useful benchmark because it combines creativity with a precise notion of correctness. You can ask a question that requires a genuinely new idea, but once you have a proof, you can check whether the reasoning holds together. That combination is quite rare.

And you can make the problems progressively harder. At one end, you have exercises where the model may recognize a familiar pattern. At the other, you have problems where it needs to explore, try an approach, realize that it doesn’t work, and find a different path. That gives you a way to study whether the model can sustain reasoning beyond something it has already seen.

Of course, mathematics isn’t all of intelligence. But it gives us a particularly clean setting in which to ask: can this model actually make progress on a difficult problem?

sol-6.1.text:
I think mathematics has this very useful combination: it requires creativity, but there’s also a clear standard for whether you’re right. You can have an idea that sounds beautiful and convincing, but ultimately the proof has to work. So it gives us a way to distinguish something that merely sounds intelligent from something that can actually carry an argument through.

And you can keep asking new questions. You don’t have to restrict yourself to problems that people have already solved and written down. That makes it possible to probe whether a model can bring familiar ideas together in an unfamiliar situation, find an approach, and work through the consequences.

Of course, mathematics is only one aspect of intelligence. But it’s a particularly clean setting for studying reasoning, because you can examine both the answer and the steps that justify it.
